unit.title: Teaching databases and data engineering at university

video.title: Indexing and query processing: B-trees, cost and query plans
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Salma - statistics lecturer, Cairo University (main character)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: On results day, the student portal takes eight seconds to show one student's grades. The query is one line. After a single change, it takes three milliseconds. What changed?
Today: why a query on a million rows can take seconds or milliseconds, how B-tree indexes work, and how to teach students to read a query plan.
An index is a separate structure that maps key values to row locations. Without one, the database scans every row. With one, it jumps almost straight to the rows it needs.

A B-tree keeps keys sorted in wide nodes, each holding hundreds of keys. Because the tree is so wide, it stays very shallow. A million rows need only three or four levels, so three or four page reads.
The portal filtered grades by student ID, but only the grade ID was indexed. Every request scanned the whole table. One create index statement fixed it.

Every index speeds some reads but slows every write, because it must be updated too. It also takes space. And an index on a column with only two values rarely helps, since the planner will scan anyway.

Students often think indexes are magic or that more is always better. Give them a large table and have them run EXPLAIN before and after adding an index. Measuring both read and write time makes the trade-off concrete.
Quick check! A B-tree holds about two hundred keys per node. Roughly how many levels does it need for eight million rows?
Three: two hundred cubed is eight million. That is why indexed lookups stay fast as tables grow by orders of magnitude.
In the app, open the index lab. Run the same lookup with and without an index and count how many rows each method touches.
Your turn. A column holds only yes or no, evenly split. Will an index on it usually speed up a filter on that column?
Usually not: half the rows match, so scanning is cheaper. Remember: B-trees stay shallow, every index costs writes and space, and EXPLAIN shows what the planner decided.

scenes.narration: Try it in your next lecture: load a million-row table and let pairs run one slow query. They read the plan, add one index and run it again. Then they measure how much slower inserts became.

checkpoints.prompt: About 200 keys per node. Roughly how many levels for 8 million rows?
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: wide nodes keep the tree shallow; 200³ is eight million, so three levels.

checkpoints.prompt: A yes/no column, evenly split. Will an index usually speed a filter on it?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: half the rows match, so a scan is cheaper.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: low selectivity means the planner scans anyway.
